opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I think people really underestimate. There's this intuition that if the underlying process is smooth, if you're just adding a bit more compute, a bit more data, a few more IQ points, then the outputs must also be smooth. But that's just not how the world works. Smooth inputs produce discontinuous outputs all the time.

Think about water. You cool it one degree at a time, nothing much happens, nothing much happens, and then suddenly it's ice. Phase transitions are everywhere in nature. And I think intelligence is very much like this, because what matters isn't some abstract scalar of "how smart are you," it's whether you cross certain thresholds where whole new strategies become available to you.

Look at humans versus chimps. Our brains aren't some magical new architecture. They're a scaled-up primate brain, roughly three times bigger, with some tweaks. On the biological level, that's a pretty continuous change. But the outcome? Chimps are where they were a million years ago, and we went to the moon. The difference isn't that we're three times better at chimp things. It's that somewhere along the way we crossed a threshold where we could do language, cumulative culture, abstraction, science. Once you can write things down and build on what the last generation figured out, you're playing a completely different game. That's a discontinuity in capability coming out of a fairly continuous change in hardware.

And I expect the same thing with AI. You have a system that's getting a little better at coding, a little better at planning, a little better at long-horizon tasks. And for a while it looks like a nice useful tool. But at some point it gets good enough to meaningfully do AI research itself, or to coordinate copies of itself, or to acquire resources without a human in the loop. Each of those is a threshold. And crossing one of them doesn't feel like plus one percent. It feels like the whole system changed character.

The really nasty part is that you often can't see these thresholds coming from the inside of the smooth curve. Benchmarks go up gradually, the loss goes down gradually, and everyone goes, "See, it's all continuous, nothing to worry about." But the loss curve doesn't tell you what the system can do in the world. It's like watching a kid's vocabulary grow word by word and concluding they'll never write a novel, because there was never a "novel-writing jump" in the vocabulary count.

So when people tell me, "Don't worry, we'll see it coming, it'll be gradual," my response is: gradual in what? Gradual in the metric you happened to be measuring, maybe. But the things that actually matter, like can this thing outmaneuver us, can it improve itself, can it hide what it's doing, those can flip very quickly. And if you're relying on getting a warning shot and then reacting, you're betting your entire civilization on there being a nice smooth ramp on the exact axis that kills you. I really don't want to make that bet.

r001.rationale: It says smooth increases in compute, data, or intelligence can cross thresholds that make new strategies and capabilities available.

r002.rationale: It identifies writing things down and building on what previous generations learned as a way cumulative culture enables new capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of teaching each human a fact with propagating learning across deployed AI instances.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend explicitly identifying what remains confusing when reasoning about artificial superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It notes that benchmarks and smooth metrics may not reveal real-world capabilities, but does not state that current scientific understanding cannot precisely account for possible capability discontinuities.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the key confusion here is that people conflate the smoothness of the input with the smoothness of the output. You can have a perfectly continuous increase in some underlying quantity and still get wildly discontinuous behavior out the other side. Water heats up smoothly, degree by degree, and then at a very specific point it boils. Nothing weird happened to the heat. The phase transition is a property of the system, not of the thing you were turning up.

Intelligence is like that, and the clearest example we have is us. The genetic distance between a human and a chimpanzee is tiny. Brain size went up by some modest factor, there were a few architectural tweaks, nothing that looks like a miracle on the input side. And the output side is that one species builds particle accelerators and the other one is in a zoo. That's not a 3x difference in capability. That's not a difference you can even measure on the same axis. Chimps don't have a slightly worse version of the Manhattan Project. They have zero of it.

And the reason, I think, is that a lot of what we call capabilities are threshold phenomena. Certain things only become possible once you can hold enough in working memory, or chain enough steps of reasoning together, or model another agent well enough to coordinate with them. Below the threshold you get essentially nothing, above it you get the whole thing. Language is like this. Recursive planning is like this. Being able to model your own cognition and improve it is like this. You don't get half a culture.

Then there's the second layer, which is that once you cross one of those thresholds, the capabilities compose. Writing lets you accumulate knowledge across generations, which lets you do science, which lets you build tools that make you effectively smarter, and so on. So even a smooth gain in the raw substrate gets amplified through this compounding loop into something that looks, from the outside, like it came out of nowhere.

Now apply this to AI. People look at the scaling curves and say, look, loss goes down smoothly, so capabilities must come smoothly too. But loss is the temperature, not the boiling. We've already seen this empirically. You train a model on a smooth curve and then at some size it suddenly does arithmetic, or in-context learning, or whatever. The underlying metric didn't jump. The behavior did. And that's a toy version of the thing I'm worried about at the high end, which is that there's some threshold, I don't know where it is, nobody does, past which a system can do the full autonomous science-and-engineering loop, including on itself. And on the other side of that threshold the world looks completely different, and you don't get a warning on the loss curve.

So when people say, well, progress has been continuous so far, so we'll see it coming, I think they have the burden of proof exactly backwards. Continuous progress is precisely the regime in which you get surprised. The one time this happened before in history, with us, nobody saw it coming either, least of all the chimps.

r001.rationale: It says smooth increases in an underlying quantity can produce discontinuous behavior, using boiling and intelligence as examples.

r002.rationale: It explains that writing lets knowledge accumulate across generations, enabling science, tool-building, and further capability gains.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of teaching facts to every human with the ease of propagating learning across deployed AI instances.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend explicitly identifying what remains confusing when reasoning about artificial superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It says the location of a possible AI capability threshold is unknown, but does not state that current scientific understanding of intelligence cannot support precise accounts of such discontinuities.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between a continuous change in some underlying variable and a continuous change in what you can actually do. Those are very different things. You can improve a system smoothly, and then suddenly it crosses a threshold where some task becomes possible.

Think about a research problem. If you’re slightly below the level needed to solve it, you might make no progress for years. If you’re slightly above it, you solve it, and that solution gives you access to a whole new set of tools. The underlying improvement could be small, but the consequences are enormous.

Humans are an interesting example because our individual cognitive abilities haven’t changed that dramatically over the period in which we went from very simple technologies to computers and spaceflight. We developed language, accumulated knowledge, built institutions—things that let cognitive abilities compound. There are feedback loops there.

With artificial intelligence, the question is whether you cross thresholds that enable similar feedback loops, perhaps much faster. Can the system do useful research? Can it improve the tools it uses to do research? Can it contribute to improving the next system? You don’t need to assume some magical jump in intelligence for the capabilities to change very sharply.

That doesn’t establish that a sudden transition will happen. There could be bottlenecks everywhere. But ‘the inputs are improving continuously, therefore the outcomes will improve continuously’ just isn’t a valid inference. What matters is where the thresholds are and what happens once you cross them.

r001.rationale: It says a system can improve smoothly and then cross a threshold where a task suddenly becomes possible, making capability change sharply.

r002.rationale: It names language, accumulated knowledge, and institutions as mechanisms that let human cognitive abilities compound.

r003.rationale: It does not contrast teaching facts to every human with propagating learning across deployed AI instances.

r004.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about thresholds and bottlenecks but does not recommend identifying what remains confusing.

r005.rationale: It notes uncertainty about whether a sudden transition will happen, but does not say current scientific understanding of intelligence cannot support precise accounts of discontinuities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between a system changing continuously and the consequences of that system changing continuously. Those are very different claims. You can improve some underlying capability smoothly, but then cross a threshold where something qualitatively new becomes possible.

Think about solving a problem that requires ten steps. If you’re slightly unreliable at every step, you almost never get to the end. As your reliability improves, there can be a fairly narrow range where you go from basically never solving it to solving it consistently. Nothing discontinuous happened to the underlying machinery, but the useful capability looks like it appeared quite suddenly.

And intelligence operates in an environment full of thresholds. Can you understand this particular idea? Can you write a working program? Can you do research well enough to improve your own tools? Once you can do something, that can open up opportunities that weren’t available before, which can feed back into further improvement.

Humans are an illustration of why I don’t find this possibility particularly strange. Individually, we have limitations, but language, accumulated knowledge, and cooperation let us do things that no other animal comes close to doing. That doesn’t require some magical discontinuity in the laws of physics.

So continuous improvements in an AI don’t imply a smooth, predictable increase in its impact. They also don’t prove that there will be a sudden explosion. The point is that you have to examine the thresholds and feedback loops. You can’t settle the question just by saying that the underlying curve is continuous.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says smooth improvements in an underlying capability can cross thresholds that make qualitatively new abilities possible.

r002.rationale: It mentions language, accumulated knowledge, and cooperation, but does not identify improved cultural transmission as a mechanism for further accumulating capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not compare teaching facts to humans with propagating learning across deployed AI instances.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend identifying what remains confusing when reasoning about artificial superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It says a continuous underlying curve cannot settle the question, but does not state that current scientific understanding is insufficient for precise accounts of capability discontinuities.
